name: Collecting Emissions Data
title: Collecting Emissions Data
answer: Collecting emissions data covers the activity and factor data needed to calculate greenhouse gas emissions across an organization's chosen boundary. It includes Scope 1 sources such as fuel combustion in owned boilers and vehicles, Scope 2 purchased electricity, heat, steam and cooling, and Scope 3 categories such as purchased goods and services, business travel, employee commuting, waste and downstream use. The work starts with an organizational boundary decision, whether operational control, financial control or equity share, and a reporting period. Data can be site level, asset level, invoice level or spend level, and the right granularity depends on materiality and the intended use of the inventory. Collecting it means reaching into utility bills, fuel logs, meter readings, procurement records, travel bookings, supplier questionnaires and lease documents.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Collecting emissions data covers the activity and factor data needed to calculate greenhouse gas emissions across an organization's chosen boundary. It includes Scope 1 sources such as fuel combustion in owned boilers and vehicles, Scope 2 purchased electricity, heat, steam and cooling, and Scope 3 categories such as purchased goods and services, business travel, employee commuting, waste and downstream use. The work starts with an organizational boundary decision, whether operational control, financial control or equity share, and a reporting period. Data can be site level, asset level, invoice level or spend level, and the right granularity depends on materiality and the intended use of the inventory. Collecting it means reaching into utility bills, fuel logs, meter readings, procurement records, travel bookings, supplier questionnaires and lease documents.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The collection layer usually sits on top of existing business systems rather than replacing them. Electricity and gas data come from utility portals, interval meters, building management systems and submetering networks, while fuel and fleet data come from fuel cards, telematics and maintenance records. Procurement and spend data come from ERP systems, accounts payable and supplier management platforms, and travel data come from corporate booking tools and expense systems. Teams often stage this data in a data warehouse or a carbon accounting platform, then connect it to emission factor libraries such as DEFRA, EPA or IEA datasets. Spreadsheets remain common for smaller sources, manual adjustments and audit trails, even when a dedicated platform is in place.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method begins with a source map that links each emissions category to a data owner, a system of record and a collection frequency. Activity data is extracted, cleaned and matched to the correct unit, period and facility, then multiplied by an emission factor to produce carbon dioxide equivalent. Where supplier-specific data is unavailable, teams use average data, spend-based factors or a hybrid approach, and they record which method was used for each line. Machine learning and rules-based automation help classify invoice line items, extract meter readings from documents, detect outliers and match supplier records at scale. Controls include reconciliations to financial data, review of factor versions, documented assumptions and a clear trail from reported total back to source evidence.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in emissions data collection turn on provenance, permission and defensibility. Organizations need the right to use supplier, utility, travel and payroll data for carbon reporting, and they need to respect confidentiality, data protection and contractual limits on onward sharing. Provenance means keeping the original document, the extraction method, the factor source, the calculation logic and the reviewer identity for every material figure. Risks include double counting, omitted sources, stale factors, restatements, greenwashing claims and assurance findings, all of which can damage credibility with regulators, investors and customers. Good practice is version control, role-based access, retention rules and a documented path from raw evidence to the reported inventory.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more frequent, more granular and more automated collection. Smart meters, IoT sensors, telematics and satellite data are reducing reliance on annual estimates, while supplier portals and digital product passports aim to push primary data further up the value chain. AI tools are likely to take on more document extraction, classification, anomaly detection and gap filling, but estimates will not disappear because many Scope 3 sources remain indirect. Regulatory and assurance expectations are converging on traceable, comparable and auditable data, which increases expectations for provenance and internal controls. The practical result is a shift from an annual reporting exercise to a continuous data pipeline with human review at the points that matter.
